passages.title: Snow Day
sentences: Snow fell all night.
In the morning, the radio said school was closed.
Sam cheered.
He ran outside with Pixel and threw snowballs.
Grandma Rose looked out the window and sighed.
Her car was under a big pile of snow.
She had to dig it out to get to the bakery.
Sam saw her and got a second shovel.

passages.title: Same Rain, Two Feelings
sentences: The Harbor Hawks had a big soccer match on a Saturday in November.
But on Saturday morning, rain poured down, and the field turned to mud.
The coach sent a text to say the match was canceled.
Ana stared at the rain on the window.
She had practiced her corner kicks all week.
"Now I have to wait two more weeks," she said.
Ben was on the couch with his game controller.
He was tired from a long week of tests.
He smiled and pulled a blanket over his legs.
"A rest day sounds great to me," he said.
The twins looked at each other.
It was the same rain, but they felt two different ways.

passages.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
sentences: A country mouse lived in a quiet field.
One day, his cousin from the town came to visit.
The country mouse served beans, corn and cool water.
"This food is so plain," said the town mouse. "Come to town with me!"
In town, the mice ate cake and cheese at a big table.
But the house was loud.
Doors banged, dogs barked, and people walked past all night.
The country mouse jumped at every bang.
"I love the bright lights and the fancy food," said the town mouse.
"I would rather eat beans in a quiet place," said the country mouse.
The next morning, he went home to his field.

credit.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Ferry Ride
sentences: On Friday, Sam took the ferry to his cousin's town by himself for the first time.
His mom walked him to the dock and gave him his ticket.
"Aunt Lucy will meet you on the other side," she said.
Sam had wanted to do this for months.
He had studied the ferry map and knew every stop.
As the ferry pulled away, he grinned and waved.
Then his stomach felt tight.
He checked his ticket three times.
He looked at the clock on the wall again and again.
What if Aunt Lucy was late?
Sam took out his map and found the dock where he would get off.
When the ferry bumped the dock, he saw Aunt Lucy waving.
He let out a long breath and waved back.

passages.title: Kai's News
sentences: Ben's best friend, Kai, lived two houses away.
They walked to school together every day.
One night, Kai came over with big news.
His mom had a new job in a city far up the coast, and they were moving in June.
Kai talked fast about his new house.
It had a big yard and a room just for him.
Then he got quiet.
"I'll miss walking to school with you," he said.
Ben looked at the floor.
His throat felt tight, and he stayed quiet for a long time.
Then he had an idea.
"We can play our game online every Friday," he said.
Kai smiled. "And you can visit me in the summer."
They shook hands.

passages.title: The Fisherman and the Little Fish
sentences: A fisherman sat on the rocks by the sea from morning until evening.
All day long, he caught only one fish, and it was very small.
As he reached for his basket, the little fish spoke.
"Please put me back in the sea," it said. "I am too small to make a good supper."
"If you let me go, I will grow big and fat."
"Then you can come back next year and catch me again."
The fisherman thought about this for a while.
"You may be right that you will grow," he said. "But I am hungry tonight."
"The sea is very big, and I may never find you again."
"A small supper tonight is better than a big supper that I might never get."
So he put the little fish in his basket and walked home.

credit.title: The Fisherman and the Little Fish
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Solo
sentences: Every spring, the Grade 6 band and the Grade 7 band start their concert with one song that they play together, and that song has a short solo that can be played on any instrument.
This year, Maya and Leo both auditioned for it.
On Friday afternoon, the band teacher pinned a list to the music room door.
Next to the word "Solo," it said "Maya Brooks."
Maya read the list twice.
She grinned, and then she pressed her hand against her stomach.
She had wanted this solo since September, but she had never performed alone in front of three hundred people.
"What if my hands start shaking?" she whispered.
Leo was standing right behind her, and he read the list too.
He had practiced the solo every evening for two weeks.
For a moment, he looked down at his shoes without saying anything.
Then he tapped Maya on the shoulder.
"Honestly, you played it better than I did," he said. "I am happy for you, and I am also a little disappointed."
Maya nodded slowly. "I am excited, and I am nervous too," she admitted.
"Could you sit somewhere I can see you on concert night?"
Leo grinned. "I will be at the drums, right behind the flutes," he said. "That is where I always sit when our two bands play together."

passages.title: The Robot at the Café
sentences: On Monday, the Lighthouse Café got a new helper: a robot that carried plates from the kitchen to the tables.
It was about as tall as a kitchen stool and had three shelves for plates.
Sensors on its front helped it stop before it bumped into a chair or a person.
When it reached the right table, it played a short tune and waited for the customer to lift off the food.
Priya came in after school and watched it for half an hour.
She drew a map of its path around the tables and timed each trip with her watch.
"It turns so smoothly," she said. "I want to build one like it for the robot fair."
Grandma Rose came in later for her usual cup of tea, but she did not smile at the robot.
For years, Mrs. Lin, the owner, had carried the tea over herself and stopped to chat.
Now the robot rolled up, played its tune and waited.
"It is clever," Grandma Rose said, "but it does not ask me how the bakery is doing."
Mrs. Lin felt two ways about the robot.
She no longer had to carry heavy trays across the room, so her back did not ache at the end of the day.
But she missed stopping at each table for a quick chat.
So she made a new plan: the robot would carry the plates, and she would walk over afterward to say hello.
The next day, Grandma Rose got her tea from the robot and a friendly chat from Mrs. Lin.

passages.title: Lights Out at Nine
sentences: For many years, the night sky above Harbor Town had a dull orange glow.
Bright street lights, shop signs and the floodlights at the skate park sent light upward into the sky as well as down onto the ground.
Scientists call this light pollution.
The extra light makes the whole sky glow, and that glow hides fainter stars from view.
Astronomers at the observatory on Lantern Peaks noticed that they could see fewer stars every year.
In March, the town council voted to approve a new dark-sky plan.
Every street light would get a metal shield that aimed its light down at the ground instead of up at the sky.
Shop signs would switch off automatically at ten o'clock every evening.
The floodlights at the skate park, which used to stay on until eleven, would now switch off at nine.
Maya was thrilled, because she loved to draw the constellations, and the astronomers predicted that the town would soon see many more stars.
Leo was not thrilled at all.
In summer, he usually skated until the floodlights went out, because the evenings were cool and the park was quiet.
"Now I lose two hours of skating every night," he complained to Maya. "The stars were fine before."
"The stars were not fine," Maya replied. "We just could not see most of them."
On the first night of the new plan, Maya invited Leo to walk up to the lookout with her after the skate park closed.
When they reached the top of the hill, Leo stopped walking and stared upward in silence.
A pale band of light stretched across the entire sky, made by the light of billions of distant stars.
"Is that the Milky Way?" he asked, and Maya nodded.
On the walk home, Leo admitted that the sky was amazing, but he still wished the skate park had one more hour of light.
Maya suggested that they could ask the council for special lamps that shine only down onto the ramps.

passages.title: A Mine by the River
sentences: Copper is a reddish metal that is found in certain kinds of rock under the ground.
It carries electricity well, so it is used in phone chargers, computers, electric cars and the wires inside our homes.
To get copper, a company digs a mine, crushes the rock and separates the metal from the stone.
When a company plans a new mine near a town, people in the town often feel very differently about it.
Some people are glad, because a mine brings jobs that pay well, and the money helps local shops, schools and roads.
Young people who might have moved away to find work may be able to stay near their families.
Other people are worried.
Mines can be noisy and dusty, and big trucks carry rock along roads where children walk to school.
If waste from a mine leaks into a river, it can harm fish and the water that people and farms need.
Some people also love the forests and hills as they are, and they do not want them dug up.
Many people feel both ways at once.
A worker might want a job at the mine but also want to keep fishing in a clean river with her children.
To protect the land and water, many places have rules for mines.
In those places, a mine must test the water often, and when it closes, the company must cover the bare ground with soil and plant new trees and grass.
Before a new mine is allowed to open, people in the town can often go to public meetings, ask questions and share their views.
Hearing every side does not make the choice easy, but it can help a town make a choice that more people can accept.

passages.title: The Cock and the Jewel
sentences: A hungry rooster was scratching in the farmyard dirt for food.
His claws hit something hard and smooth.
It was a red jewel, and it sparkled in the sun.
The rooster looked at the jewel and shook his head.
"People think you are a treasure," he said to it.
"A jeweler would be glad to find you and sell you in her shop."
"But you are no use to me, because I cannot eat you."
"To me, one grain of corn is worth more than a jewel."
Then he left the jewel in the dirt and went back to looking for corn.

credit.title: The Cock and the Jewel
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Train Horn
sentences: On Saturday, Sam and Maya waited at the train crossing by the harbor.
Sam wanted to see the long freight train.
Maya wanted to draw it for her new comic.
Soon the red lights flashed, and the gate came down.
The train blew its horn as it came close.
Sam grinned and counted the cars.
"That horn is the best sound in the world!" he shouted.
Maya put her hands over her ears and stepped back.
The horn was much too loud for her.
After the train left, Sam had an idea.
Next time, they could watch from the hill behind the station.
The horn would sound softer there, and Maya could still draw the train.

passages.title: The Gnat and the Bull
sentences: A gnat is a tiny fly, smaller than a grain of rice.
One hot afternoon, a gnat flew across a wide field and landed on the horn of a big bull.
He sat there for a long time and rested his wings.
He looked out over the field and felt very important.
"I am sitting on the biggest animal in this whole field," he thought.
"The bull must be amazed to have a visitor like me."
At last, the gnat got ready to leave.
He buzzed loudly next to the bull's ear.
"Excuse me," he said politely. "I am sorry if I was too heavy for you."
"I will fly away now, so you can rest."
The bull kept chewing his grass.
"I did not even know you were there," he said calmly. "I will not notice when you go, either."
The gnat flew away without another word.

credit.title: The Gnat and the Bull
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Swallow and the Crow
sentences: On a warm spring morning, a swallow landed on a fence next to a crow.
The swallow's feathers were shiny blue on top and soft orange underneath.
She looked at the crow's stiff black feathers and shook her head.
"Your feathers are so dull," she said. "You should take more pride in how you look, like I do."
The crow did not seem upset.
"Your feathers are very pretty in the spring sunshine," she replied.
"But every fall, you fly far away to warmer places."
"You have never seen this farm in winter, when the snow is deep and the wind is cold."
"My thick black feathers keep me warm all winter long, so I can stay here the whole year."
"In fact, winter is my favorite season of all."
The swallow had never thought about winter before.
She looked at the crow's feathers again, and this time she looked more carefully.

credit.title: The Swallow and the Crow
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Feathers on the Raptors
sentences: Ben and Leo had played Dino Valley every Friday for a year.
In the game, each player builds a park and takes care of the dinosaurs.
This Friday, a new update gave the raptors, the fastest dinosaurs in the game, a brand-new look.
Now they had brown and white feathers on their arms and tails.
Ben cheered when he saw them.
"Scientists found out that raptors really had feathers," he said. "Now the game is right!"
Leo frowned at the screen.
"They look like giant chickens," he said. "I liked the old green scales better."
Ben opened his dinosaur book and showed Leo a picture of a raptor's arm bone.
It had a row of tiny bumps where feathers were once attached.
Leo studied the picture for a long time.
"Okay, that is pretty cool," he admitted. "But I still miss the old scales a little."
Then he found a setting that turned his raptors' feathers bright blue, and he grinned.

passages.title: The Seal on the Ramp
sentences: Early on Sunday, a gray harbor seal climbed out of the water and lay down on the boat ramp.
It stretched out in the warm sun and closed its eyes.
A harbor worker put up a rope, because seals need plenty of space when they rest.
Soon a crowd gathered behind the rope.
Sam and Priya were in the crowd, and they could not stop smiling.
"Look at its long whiskers!" Priya whispered.
A woman with a small fishing boat was not smiling.
She needed the ramp to put her boat in the water.
"I wanted to go fishing two hours ago," she said with a sigh.
But she knew the seal was resting, and she did not want to bother it.
So she sat on a bench, poured a cup of coffee and watched the seal too.
At noon, the seal slid back into the water, and the crowd clapped.
The woman clapped too, and then she backed her boat down the ramp.

passages.title: The Finish Line
sentences: A marathon is a running race that is about 42 kilometers, or 26 miles, long.
Big city marathons can have more than thirty thousand runners.
The fastest runners finish in just over two hours.
Many others take five or six hours, and some walk part of the way.
At the finish line, runners feel many different things.
The winner runs through a ribbon and raises both arms in the air.
A runner near the back may feel just as proud, because she reached a goal she trained for all year.
Many runners feel two things at the same time.
Their legs ache, and they are very tired.
But they also feel proud that they did not give up.
Volunteers hand each finisher a medal and a bottle of water.
For most runners, the medal means finishing, not winning.

passages.title: The Man and the Lion
sentences: Long ago, a man and a lion were traveling together along a forest path.
To pass the time, they began to argue about which of them was stronger and smarter.
"People are the greatest of all creatures," said the man. "We build cities, bridges and ships, and we can solve problems that no animal can solve."
"Lions are greater," the lion replied calmly. "We are faster and stronger than any person, and every animal in the forest respects us."
Neither of them would agree, so they continued walking in silence.
After a while, the path led into a town square with an enormous stone statue in the middle.
The statue showed a tall, powerful man standing proudly, with a lion lying quietly at his feet.
The man pointed at it and smiled.
"There!" he said. "That statue proves that people are stronger than lions."
The lion studied the statue for a long moment, and then he laughed a deep, rumbling laugh.
"That statue was carved by a person," he said. "Naturally, the person who carved it put a person on top."
"If lions knew how to carve stone, every statue in this town would show a lion standing proudly, with a man at its feet."
The man opened his mouth to answer, but then he closed it again.
For the first time, he wondered how the same story might sound if someone else were telling it.

credit.title: The Man and the Lion
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Winning Kick
sentences: The spring tournament game had ended in a tie, so the two teams had to decide the winner with penalty kicks.
Each team chose five players to shoot, and Coach Novak picked Ana to take the last kick for her team.
Ana had practiced penalty kicks after school every day for a month, always aiming for the low corners of the net.
As she set the ball on the spot, she looked up at the goalkeeper and recognized her.
They had met at summer camp, shared a cabin for two weeks and become good friends.
Ana took a deep breath and kicked the ball hard toward the left corner.
The goalkeeper dived the other way, and the ball rolled into the back of the net.
Ana's teammates rushed over, shouting and jumping, and Ben lifted her off the ground.
A moment later, the referee blew the whistle to end the game, and Ana's team had won.
While her team celebrated, Ana glanced back at the goal.
Her friend was sitting on the grass with her gloves in her lap, staring at the ground.
Ana's smile faded a little.
She was proud of her kick, but she also knew exactly how her friend was feeling.
She jogged over and held out her hand.
"That was a great game," she said. "You stopped three of our best shots in the first half."
Her friend looked up, took a long breath and smiled a small smile.
"Next year, I am going to guess the right way," she said, and Ana laughed as she helped her up.

passages.title: The Dropped Can
sentences: At the school open house, the robotics club showed its newest machine: a robot arm that sorted recycling.
A camera looked at each object on a moving belt, and then the arm picked it up and dropped it into the right bin.
Cans went into the blue bin, and paper went into the green one.
Priya and Ben had helped build the arm for six weeks, and about forty parents and students had come to watch.
The first five objects landed perfectly, and the crowd clapped.
Then the arm picked up a shiny soda can, lifted it high and let go too early.
The can missed both bins, bounced off the edge of the stage and rolled under the front row of chairs.
A few people laughed.
Ben's face turned hot and red, and he stared at the floor.
He wished he could switch the robot off and walk away.
Priya laughed too, but she leaned forward with interest.
"Did you see that?" she whispered. "It only happened with the shiny can. I bet the stage lights are bouncing off the metal and confusing the camera."
Ms. Ortiz asked the crowd if they would like to see how engineers find and fix a problem, and many people nodded.
Priya dimmed the bright stage lights, and Ben placed another shiny can on the belt.
This time, the arm dropped it neatly into the blue bin, and the crowd clapped even louder than before.
Afterward, Ben said that the dropped can was the most embarrassing moment of his whole year.
"But it was also the best part of the show," he added, "because everyone got to see us solve a real problem."

passages.title: Drums in the Garage
sentences: Every day when he got home from school, Leo practiced his drums in the garage for one hour.
The band had a concert in three weeks, and he was learning a fast new rhythm for the last song.
He loved how loud and strong the beat sounded inside the garage.
One afternoon, someone knocked on the garage door.
It was his neighbor, who drove a freight train all night and slept during the day.
She looked tired, and her voice was quiet.
"I am glad you love music," she said, "but I go to sleep at two, and your drums wake me up every afternoon."
Leo felt two things at once.
He felt bad that he had been waking her up, because he had never thought about anyone sleeping during the day.
But he also felt frustrated, because the concert was close and he needed every minute of practice.
His neighbor felt two ways too: she did not want to stop a young drummer from getting better, but she could not drive the train safely without enough sleep.
They sat on the front steps and talked about it.
On weekdays, Leo would practice on a rubber practice pad, which makes a soft tap instead of a loud bang.
On Saturday mornings, when his neighbor was awake, he could play the full drum kit as loudly as he liked.
Three weeks later, she came to the concert and sat in the front row.
When the last song ended, she clapped harder than anyone else in the gym.

passages.title: Ten Flags at Lantern Peaks
sentences: On a Saturday in May, Sam and Priya entered the team orienteering race at Lantern Peaks.
In orienteering, teams use a map and a compass to locate orange and white flags hidden across the hills.
At each flag, they punch a card to prove they were there, and the fastest team to find every flag wins.
Sam carried the map, and Priya carried the compass and a stopwatch.
The fourth flag was on the opposite side of a steep, rocky hill.
Most teams scrambled straight over the top, but Sam studied the map carefully and chose a trail that curved around the bottom of the hill.
The trail was longer, but the ground was flat, and it would lead them directly to the flag.
The plan worked perfectly, and they located all ten flags without a single wrong turn.
But when they crossed the finish line, the results board showed that they had finished eighth out of ten teams.
Priya frowned at her stopwatch, which showed that they had been twelve minutes slower than the winning team.
"Climbing over the hill would definitely have been faster," she said.
Sam could not stop grinning.
"We found all ten flags, and we never got lost once," he said. "That is the best I have ever done with a map."
Priya considered this for a moment, and then she smiled.
"You are right, and I am proud of that too," she said. "But next year, I want to try the hill."
Sam laughed and suggested that they could practice on the steep hill behind the observatory first.

passages.title: Grandma Rose's New Bread
sentences: For as long as Sam could remember, Rose's Bakery had sold the same soft white bread every morning.
In the spring, Grandma Rose decided to try something new.
For six weeks, she tested a brown loaf made with whole wheat flour, oats and sunflower seeds.
Whole wheat flour is made from the entire grain, so it has more fiber than white flour, and the seeds add a nutty crunch.
When the recipe was finally just right, she replaced the white bread with the new loaf.
Sam loved it from the first bite, and so did many customers.
But on Monday, Mr. Okafor came in for his usual white loaf and stared at the shelf in surprise.
"I make my lunch sandwiches with your white bread every day," he said. "This new bread is good, but it is not the same."
Two other customers who had shopped there for years said almost the same thing that week.
That night, Grandma Rose sat at the kitchen table with Sam.
"I feel proud of the new bread, because I worked hard to get it right," she said.
"But I also feel bad, because some of my oldest customers miss the bread they have loved for years."
Sam thought for a while, and then he suggested a plan.
The bakery could sell the new loaf every day and bake the white bread again on Mondays and Thursdays.
Grandma Rose liked the idea, and the next morning she taped a sign about it to the window.
The following Monday, Mr. Okafor bought a white loaf for his sandwiches and a brown one to try at home.

passages.title: The Quiet Ferry
sentences: For twenty years, Captain Ruth Lane had steered the Harbor Town ferry across the bay, and she knew every sound its old diesel engine made.
In September, the town replaced that ferry with a new electric one.
Instead of burning fuel, the new ferry runs on large batteries, which are recharged through a thick cable at the dock while passengers get on and off.
It produces no exhaust smoke, and its motors are so quiet that passengers can hear the waves splashing against the hull.
Sam rode the new ferry on its very first morning, and he could hardly stand still.
He had read about electric ferries for months, and he asked the captain dozens of questions about the batteries, the charging cable and the motors.
"It is the most amazing boat I have ever seen," he told Grandma Rose, who had come along for the ride.
Grandma Rose agreed that the air smelled cleaner, and she was delighted that she could finally hear the seagulls during the trip.
Captain Lane felt two ways about the change.
She was proud that Harbor Town had chosen a cleaner boat, and she enjoyed the calm, smooth ride.
But she also missed the deep rumble of the old engine, because for twenty years that sound had told her exactly how the ferry was running.
Without it, she had to learn to read new signals, such as the numbers on a bright screen beside the wheel.
On the first few trips, she checked that screen every few minutes.
After the last trip of the day, Sam found the captain standing quietly at the rail, looking at the old ferry tied up across the harbor.
"Do you miss it?" he asked.
"I do," she said with a small smile. "I can miss the old ferry and still be glad about the new one. Both feelings are true."
Then she showed Sam how the screen counted down the minutes until the batteries were full again.

passages.title: The Garnet
sentences: On a warm Saturday in July, Maya and Leo visited the Ridgeway Mine Museum in Lantern Peaks.
Behind the museum stood a long wooden trough called a sluice, where water flowed slowly past a row of benches.
Visitors filled a screen box with sandy gravel, dipped it into the water and shook it gently until only the stones remained.
Mr. Varga, who guides the mine tours and leads the rock club, showed them how to search the wet stones for anything unusual.
Leo's screen box held nothing but plain gray pebbles and one piece of green glass.
Maya found something very different: a dark red crystal about the size of a pea, with smooth, flat sides.
Mr. Varga held it up to the sunlight and whistled softly.
"That is a garnet, and it is the best one anyone has found here all summer," he said.
He explained that the name garnet comes from an old Latin word for pomegranate, a fruit full of deep red seeds, because the crystals are often the same color.
Then Mr. Varga asked Maya a question.
"The rock club's display case at the library has no garnet in it," he said. "Would you consider lending this one to the club, so that other people can enjoy it too?"
Maya closed her hand around the stone and did not answer right away.
She wanted to keep it in her own collection box, where she could examine it every night.
But she also remembered how excited she had felt the first time she saw a real crystal in that display case.
Leo stood beside her, holding his piece of green glass.
He felt a little jealous, because he had shaken his screen box for an entire hour and found nothing special.
Still, he was genuinely glad for Maya, and he told her it was the most beautiful stone he had ever seen.
Finally, Maya decided to lend the garnet to the display case for one month, with a card that said, "Found by Maya Brooks."
After that, it would come home to her collection box.

passages.title: Coming Home from Space
sentences: Astronauts who live on the International Space Station usually stay for about six months.
During that time, they float everywhere they go, and they can look down at Earth's oceans and clouds through the windows every day.
When their mission ends, a capsule carries them back through the atmosphere, and large parachutes slow it down before it reaches the ground or the sea.
Many astronauts say that coming home brings two strong feelings at the same time.
The first feeling is joy.
After months away, they can finally hug their families, take a real shower and eat fresh fruit and vegetables whenever they like.
Many of them say they also missed simple things about Earth, like the smell of rain, the feeling of wind and the sound of birds.
The second feeling is harder to describe, because it is a kind of missing.
Some astronauts miss the fun of floating from room to room, the view of Earth below them and the close teamwork of a small crew.
Their bodies need time to adjust to gravity again, too.
In space, muscles and bones get weaker because they do not have to hold up the body's weight, even though astronauts exercise for about two hours every day.
Back on Earth, their arms and legs feel heavy, and some astronauts feel dizzy when they first try to stand up and walk.
Some say they let go of a cup or a pen and were surprised when it fell to the floor.
With help from doctors and trainers, most astronauts can walk and balance well again within a few weeks, though their bones take longer to heal.
Many of them say they would happily return to space, even though they are glad to be home.
For them, joy and missing something are not opposites, and both feelings can be true at once.

passages.title: The Return of the Sea Otters
sentences: Sea otters are furry ocean mammals that live in shallow water along rocky coasts of the North Pacific Ocean.
Unlike seals and whales, they have no thick layer of fat to keep them warm.
Instead, they have the thickest fur of any animal, with up to about one million hairs in a single square inch.
To keep their bodies warm in cold water, sea otters eat about a quarter of their body weight in food every day.
Their favorite foods include sea urchins, crabs and clams, which they often crack open with a rock while floating on their backs.
Long ago, so many sea otters were hunted for their fur that they disappeared from most of the coasts where they once lived.
Laws now protect them, and in some places they have slowly returned.
Their return has made different people feel very different ways.
Many scientists and divers are delighted.
Sea urchins eat kelp, a giant seaweed that grows in tall underwater forests, and without otters, urchins can eat a kelp forest down to bare rock.
When otters come back and eat the urchins, the kelp can grow again, and fish, seals and seabirds return to the forest too.
Some people who catch crabs and clams as their job feel worried instead.
A hungry otter can eat many crabs and clams each day, so there may be fewer left for the boats to catch and sell.
Even one person can feel two ways at once.
A crab fisher might love watching otters play beside her boat, yet still worry about how many crabs she will catch this year.

passages.title: Rain After a Dry Summer
sentences: In some summers, weeks go by without a single drop of rain.
Lawns turn brown and crunchy, rivers shrink, and farmers watch the soil in their fields dry out and crack.
A long dry period like this is called a drought.
When rain finally arrives, the same storm can bring very different feelings to different people.
For farmers, the first heavy rain after a drought is often an enormous relief.
Their corn and beans finally get the water they need, and the ponds where their cows drink begin to fill again.
Gardeners are delighted too, and so are the people who manage a town's water supply, because the lakes that hold the town's drinking water start to rise.
Other people see the same rain differently.
A family that planned a beach day all week may feel disappointed when the sky turns gray.
The owner of an ice cream stand may sell almost nothing that afternoon.
Hard, dry ground cannot soak up water quickly, so a sudden storm after a drought can run off into the streets and leave large puddles behind.
Some people even feel two ways at once.
A farmer might be thankful for the rain on her corn but frustrated that it arrived on the day she planned to cut and dry her hay.
A child might be sad that a trip to the pool was canceled and also excited to jump in the first puddles of the summer.
The rain itself is the same everywhere it falls, but what changes is what each person needs from that day.
